question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man with a background of chronic systolic ventricular dysfunction (last echocardiogram two months ago reported an ejection fraction of 28 %) and biopsy-proven compensated cirrhosis from long-standing non-alcohol-related steatohepatitis arrived via private vehicle to the emergency department just after noon complaining of three episodes of vomiting fluid he described as “rust-colored and gritty” over the preceding four hours, the largest filling nearly half of a household mixing bowl; he denied passing tarry or unusually dark stools and stated that his most recent bowel movement earlier that morning was medium brown and normally formed. He reported that the first retch occurred shortly after finishing a late breakfast and was preceded by a wave of nausea, a metallic taste, and mild epigastric pressure that had been smoldering for several days but intensified overnight. Between heaves he noted lightheadedness and clamminess but never lost consciousness, remained ambulatory, and was able to walk from the parking lot into triage without assistance. His cardiac history is complicated by two prior admissions in the past year for pulmonary congestion requiring intravenous loop diuretics; at baseline he sleeps with three pillows, can manage half a flight of stairs before pausing for breath, and takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg each morning, low-dose spironolactone, and sacubitril-valsartan titrated to guideline-directed doses. Liver-directed care is overseen by hepatology every six months; surveillance ultrasound three weeks ago revealed nodular contour without ascites, and he has never undergone endoscopic band ligation, though he was advised to begin non-selective beta-blockade two years ago to reduce portal pressure. Additional medical problems include diet-controlled type 2 diabetes and hyperuricemia treated with allopurinol. He quit cigarette smoking fifteen years ago after a twenty-pack-year exposure, drinks no alcohol since his cirrhosis was diagnosed, and denies recreational drug use. Regular medications aside from those noted include aspirin-free multivitamins and lansoprazole 30 mg daily, though he admits to missing several doses of the proton pump inhibitor this past week because his prescription lapsed. He is not on antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, corticosteroids, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Family history is notable for a father who died of myocardial infarction at 70 and a mother with rheumatoid arthritis; no relatives have had peptic ulcer disease or bleeding disorders. On review of systems he endorses progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea over several weeks but denies fever, chest pain, cough, jaundice, pruritus, ankle swelling beyond his usual trace baseline, abdominal distention, easy bruising, gingival bleeding, or hematochezia. Upon arrival—prior to placement of intravenous lines, administration of fluids, vasoactive agents, acid suppression, or antiemetics—triage vitals recorded blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg measured manually in the seated position, a regular pulse of 109 beats per minute palpated at the radial artery, respirations 20 per minute, oral temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing ambient air. The patient appeared pale, diaphoretic, and anxious yet was oriented to person, place, and time. Capillary refill exceeded three seconds; jugular venous pulsation was estimated at 8 cm above the sternal angle with the head elevated 45°. Conjunctival membranes were markedly pale, sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa dry, and spider angiomata dotted the upper chest and shoulders. Cardiac examination revealed a displaced apical impulse with an audible third heart sound but no murmurs or pericardial rub; bibasilar crackles were appreciated on lung auscultation. The abdomen was scaphoid and soft with mild tenderness to deep palpation in the epigastrium; no rebound, guarding, masses, or ascites wave was detected, and a firm blunt liver edge was palpable two centimeters below the right costal margin. There was trace bilateral ankle edema. Neurologic screening demonstrated intact cranial nerves II–XII, normal motor strength, and no asterixis. Digital rectal examination was deferred until after laboratory studies because of active retching in the triage bay. Venous blood drawn through a 20-gauge catheter before any therapy yielded hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, hematocrit 26 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, platelet count 162 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.9 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL), sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, albumin 2.9 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 64 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 118 U/L, and an international normalized ratio of 1.4. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained simultaneously demonstrated sinus tachycardia at 108 bpm with nonspecific lateral ST-segment changes but no acute ischemia. Upright chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly with mild vascular congestion and clear lung fields; supine abdominal film showed a nonspecific gas pattern without free air. No crystalloid resuscitation, blood products, proton pump inhibitors, octreotide, antibiotics, or vasoactive medications had yet been initiated; two additional large-bore peripheral lines were prepared, a type and crossmatch for four units of packed red blood cells was sent, the patient was placed on continuous cardiac monitoring, kept nil per os, and gastroenterology and hepatology services were paged for urgent endoscopic evaluation of the suspected upper gastrointestinal source of bleeding in the context of his known cardiomyopathy and chronic liver disease.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Use the pretreatment Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score:
- BUN 42 mg/dL corresponds to urea 15 mmol/L, in the 10 to <25 mmol/L band: 4 points.
- Hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL in a man (<10): 6.
- Systolic BP 94 mmHg (90–99): 2.
- Pulse 109/min (≥100): 1.
- Melena: no; the last stool was brown. Hematemesis does not score as melena: 0.
- Syncope: lightheadedness without loss of consciousness: 0.
- Hepatic disease: biopsy-proven cirrhosis: 2.
- Cardiac failure: symptomatic systolic dysfunction with ejection fraction 28%: 2.
Sum: 4 + 6 + 2 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 2 = 17.
Final answer: 17
